title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Vascular sonography addresses the diagnostic challenge of identifying arterial, venous, and lymphatic pathology in patients with suspected circulatory or lymphatic disorders, conditions commonly arising from atherosclerosis, thrombosis, inflammation, malignancy, trauma, or postoperative states. Clinical indications include limb swelling, pain, ischemic symptoms, suspected venous thromboembolism, bruit detection, and unexplained lymphadenopathy. Vascular sonography is a noninvasive imaging procedure that evaluates arterial and venous structures and lymph nodes using high-frequency sound waves. B-mode imaging characterizes vessel wall morphology, lumen patency, and lymph node architecture, while color-flow imaging assesses flow direction and patterns, and spectral Doppler quantifies blood velocity and hemodynamic indices.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Indications include evaluation of arterial stenosis, venous thrombosis, aneurysmal disease, and lymph node pathology. Relative contraindications are few and primarily involve the inability to tolerate probe compression or required positioning. Technical limitations include operator dependence, obesity, vascular calcification, and restricted acoustic windows. When performed appropriately, vascular sonography enables timely diagnosis and management. When omitted or delayed, unrecognized or progressive disease may lead to ischemia, embolization, infectious spread, or delayed oncologic diagnosis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity for healthcare professionals is designed to advance learners’ skills in correlating vascular sonographic findings with clinical presentation to optimize patient evaluation and procedural or medical management. Participants will learn procedural indications, contraindications, preparation protocols, equipment selection, and technical execution relevant to this assessment modality. Refined proficiency will strengthen clinician collaboration in interprofessional strategies addressing the health needs of individuals undergoing sonographic assessment of arterial, venous, or lymphatic pathology.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Assess patients for indications for sonographic vascular and lymphatic imaging by correlating clinical presentation, risk factors, and suspected pathology. Interpret venous sonographic findings using grayscale and Doppler assessment of lumen patency, compressibility, reflux, respiratory phasicity, and augmentation response. Differentiate common vascular and lymphatic pathologies based on their sonographic grayscale and Doppler characteristics. Collaborate with the interprofessional team to educate, treat, and monitor patients undergoing sonographic vascular and lymphatic assessment to improve health outcomes. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Introduction
content: Ultrasonography uses sound waves to generate medical diagnostic images. The portability, cost-effectiveness, radiation-free nature, dynamic imaging capability, and noninvasiveness of this assessment technique have contributed to widespread adoption over recent decades, establishing ultrasound as the first-line modality for vascular screening and diagnosis. [1] [2]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Introduction
content: Vascular ultrasound is a generalized term encompassing grayscale sonography and Doppler assessment of a wide range of arterial and venous pathologies. Commonly evaluated conditions include peripheral arterial disease, arteritis, arterial aneurysms, pseudoaneurysm, dissection, vascular malformations, venous thrombosis, and venous insufficiency. [3] Sonography also provides assessment of the lymphatic system by evaluating lymph node size, morphology, and vascular patterns. [4] [5] This activity focuses on the general principles of arterial, venous, and lymph node sonography, with application to frequently encountered vascular and lymphatic pathologies.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Initial sonographic arterial evaluation begins with grayscale ultrasound, assessing arterial wall thickness, luminal diameter, and morphological characteristics of atherosclerotic plaque, followed by Doppler assessment. [6] Doppler ultrasonography applies the Doppler shift to quantify red blood cell velocity within the vascular system. A positive Doppler shift indicates blood movement toward the transducer, whereas a negative shift indicates movement away from the transducer. The angle at which a Doppler beam intercepts moving blood flow is defined as the Doppler angle.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Vascular sonographers should scan at a Doppler angle of less than 60°. The rationale is described by the equations below, where Fd represents the frequency of the echo shifted by the Doppler effect, and Ft denotes the frequency of the initial Doppler beam prior to the shift: Doppler frequency shift (Fd) = [2 × Ft × velocity of blood × cos(Doppler angle)] / velocity of sound in tissue Rearranged for blood velocity: Velocity of blood = (Fd × velocity of sound in tissue) / [2 × Ft × cos(Doppler angle)] [7]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: In the equation for blood velocity, cos(Doppler angle) appears in the denominator. Since cos(0°) equals 1 and cos(90°) is 0, a Doppler angle near 0° produces the maximum calculated blood flow velocity. The calculated velocity decreases as the Doppler angle increases above 60° and approaches 90°, ultimately approaching 0. Estimation of the Doppler angle is operator-dependent and requires precise alignment to minimize error.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Arteries may be classified as high- or low-resistance. High-resistance vessels classically generate a triphasic waveform on Doppler assessment (see Image . Typical Triphasic Waveform). These waveforms are observed in arteries located within skeletal muscles, including the external iliac, femoral, and radial arteries, as well as the corresponding downstream branches of these vessels.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Spectral broadening may occur when blood flow becomes less laminar and more turbulent. [8] The black area between the spectral baseline and the spectral line is termed the "spectral window." "Spectral broadening" refers to the filling of the spectral window resulting from recording a multitude of velocities. [9] Red blood cells typically travel at uniform speed in high-resistance vessels unless tortuosity, branching, or pathological changes are present. Consequently, these vessels normally exhibit minimal spectral broadening. Triphasic waveforms consist of 3 classic components: An initial sharp rise in velocity during systole, followed by a rapid fall during ventricular contraction A short-duration reversal of flow occurring during early diastole A small amount of forward flow persisting in the final portion of diastole

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Low-resistance vessels typically display a monophasic waveform (see Image . Monophasic Waveform). These waveforms are found in arteries supplying organs with high oxygen demand, such as the internal carotid, renal, umbilical, and postprandial gut arteries. Unlike high-resistance vessels, these arteries and their downstream branches remain continually dilated to support increased oxygen delivery. For example, the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries exhibit low-resistance waveforms during digestion and high-resistance waveforms during fasting. [10]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: In a low-resistance waveform, 2 physiologic phases are typically visualized: a slow initial rise in velocity during systole and a gradual decrease in velocity during diastole. In contrast to high-resistance waveforms, no flow reversal occurs during systole or diastole, permitting increased tissue oxygenation.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Confusion has existed in the literature and among clinicians regarding the biphasic waveform and its interpretation. A recent consensus statement by the Societies for Vascular Ultrasound and Vascular Medicine recommends describing the classic biphasic waveform under the umbrella term “multiphasic,” which encompasses both triphasic and biphasic waveforms. Multiphasic waveforms cross the baseline. Historically, the biphasic waveform exhibited both high- and low-resistance characteristics, with a sharp upstroke, a brisk downstroke, and continued forward flow during diastole. The term "biphasic" has now been replaced with the description of an intermediate-resistance multiphasic waveform. [11] Consequently, descriptors such as high-, intermediate-, or low-resistance are considered more relevant than subtle distinctions in phasicity.

content: Resistive index, also termed "Pourcelot index," is defined by the following equation, where peak systolic velocity (PSV) and end-diastolic velocity (EDV) are measured: Resistive index = (PSV − EDV) / PSV

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: A high resistive index is observed in vasculature that is constricted or exhibits limited distensibility. Such changes may result from downstream stenosis or organ congestion, as seen in the kidney. [12] Chronic renal failure is associated with increased intrarenal arterial resistive index (>0.7) due to decreased tissue compliance. In contrast, renal artery stenosis produces a low resistive index (<0.5), resulting from dampened systolic peaks with preserved diastolic flow. Renal vein thrombosis may elevate the resistive index through reversal of diastolic arterial flow. However, a normal arterial resistive index does not definitively exclude the presence of renal vein thrombosis. [13]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Lower extremity arterial stenosis produces characteristic changes in Doppler waveform patterns. Grayscale ultrasonography is useful for detecting plaques and vessel narrowing, whereas Doppler ultrasonography categorizes the degree of stenosis. Flow velocity increases within the stenotic segment, with PSV correlating most closely with stenosis severity. Downstream from the stenotic portion, spectral broadening occurs secondary to flow turbulence. High-resistance waveforms may transition from typical triphasic patterns to low-resistance monophasic waveforms, accompanied by tardus et parvus changes. Tardus (Latin for “slow”) and parvus (Latin for “weak”) describe a delayed and attenuated PSV resulting from proximal stenosis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: A ratio of PSV within and proximal to the stenosis, termed the "PSV ratio," assists in determining stenosis severity. A PSV ratio less than 2 correlates with greater than 50% stenosis of the lower extremity artery. [14] Some clinicians use a PSV ratio greater than 3 to indicate stenosis exceeding 70%, although interpretations vary.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Arterial Sonography
content: Contrast-enhanced ultrasonography (CEUS) employing microbubble contrast agents enhances visualization of microvascular blood flow and neovascularization, improving detection of plaque vulnerability. CEUS allows more precise characterization of arterial plaques and aneurysms than conventional Doppler ultrasonography. [15]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Sonographic venous assessment using grayscale ultrasonography employs compression maneuvers to evaluate vein compressibility and luminal morphology. In acute deep vein thrombosis (DVT), the thrombus appears hypoechoic, rendering the vein noncompressible and distended. In chronic DVT, the thrombus is more echogenic and adherent, and the vein becomes irregular and contracted. [16]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Venous flow is typically low velocity compared with arterial Doppler. Flow may demonstrate phasicity due to respiration or mild pulsatility secondary to right heart motion. The portal vein exhibits low-velocity flow with phasicity related to cardiac and respiratory cycles. Normal flow is directed toward the liver and is termed "hepatopetal." Flow reversal within the portal vein, called "hepatofugal," is abnormal and indicates portal hypertension. Portal hypertension most commonly results from liver cirrhosis. Alcohol abuse is the most frequent etiology in the US. [17] Portal vein diameter exceeding 15 mm also suggests portal hypertension (see Image . Portal Hypertension).

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Hepatic veins converge on the inferior vena cava immediately inferior to the right atrium. Doppler waveforms of hepatic veins reflect cardiac motion and function. Pathologies such as tricuspid regurgitation and heart failure produce characteristic alterations in hepatic venous waveforms. In these waveforms, retrograde flow toward the transducer appears above the baseline, whereas antegrade flow into the heart, away from the transducer, appears below the baseline. [18]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Hepatic veins normally exhibit 5 waveform components. The A-wave represents the reversal of blood flow during atrial systole and may be accentuated in tricuspid regurgitation or right-sided heart failure. The C-wave is a small peak of reverse flow following the A-wave, corresponding to bulging of the tricuspid valve at the onset of ventricular contraction. This wave may be absent and is considered a normal variant.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: The S-wave denotes the dominant forward flow of atrial filling during ventricular systole. In tricuspid regurgitation, the S-wave is characteristically shortened due to reduced atrial filling from the hepatic veins secondary to regurgitant flow from the right ventricle. The S-wave is typically preserved in right heart failure. The V-wave marks the end of atrial filling, and the D-wave occurs with tricuspid valve opening, reflecting subsequent filling of both the right atrium and ventricle during atrial diastole. [19]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Peripheral veins normally exhibit low-velocity, phasic flow due to respiratory variation. [20] The Valsalva maneuver induces flow reversal within the lower extremity veins. Measurement of the duration of flow reversal assists in the evaluation of venous insufficiency. Venous reflux lasting more than 1 second in the deep veins, or 0.5 seconds at any other level, is considered clinically significant for venous insufficiency, such as varicose veins.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: Squeezing the calf or contracting surrounding lower extremity muscles produces augmentation of flow. Absence of augmentation suggests stenosis, commonly resulting from venous thrombosis. Loss of respiratory phasicity indicates proximal obstruction or stenosis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Venous Sonography
content: The deep venous system comprises the common femoral, femoral, and popliteal veins, as well as their tributaries. The superficial venous system includes the great and small saphenous veins, as well as the medial marginal vein.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Lymphatic Sonography
content: Although some studies have explored sonographic assessment of lymphatic vessels, the small size of these structures limits the role of ultrasound in lymph node evaluation. [21] Ultrasound provides a real-time, noninvasive, and widely available assessment of lymph node size and morphology. Normal lymph node echogenicity ranges from isoechoic to slightly hypoechoic relative to surrounding soft tissues. [22] Marked hypoechogenicity or anechoic regions may indicate pathologies such as infection or metastasis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Lymphatic Sonography
content: Normal lymph nodes are reniform and oval, with length exceeding thickness. [23] Abnormally shaped nodes often appear rounded or spherical. [24] Loss of smooth margins also suggests pathology. Fluid-filled lymph nodes may exhibit increased transmission and acoustic enhancement, indicative of abnormalities such as necrosis. [25]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Lymphatic Sonography
content: Vascularity is typically evaluated with Doppler sonography. Three general patterns of lymph node vascularity are described: hilar, peripheral, and mixed. [26] Reactive nodes often demonstrate prominent hilar vascularity, whereas metastatic nodes typically exhibit peripheral perfusion due to marginal tumor cell deposition. Peripheral vessels in short segments, irregular branching, or aberrant vessel placement within the node are associated with malignancy. Color and spectral Doppler provide additional hemodynamic information: benign nodes demonstrate hilar flow with a low resistive index, while malignant nodes display peripheral or mixed flow with a high resistive index. [27]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Indications
content: Indications for vascular and lymph node ultrasound are diverse and may be categorized into arterial, venous, preinterventional and postinterventional assessment, and lymph node evaluation. [28] Arterial ultrasound is useful in peripheral arterial disease, arteriovenous malformations, arteriovenous fistula, arterial dissection, pseudoaneurysms, aneurysms, stenoses, transplant evaluation, and detection of emboli. Specific arterial territories that may be assessed include renal, intracranial, carotid, and umbilical arteries, and vessels supplying the gut. Venous ultrasound assists in the evaluation of venous thrombosis, hemodialysis graft patency, venous malformations, and chronic venous disease. The portal, splenic, and hepatic veins are also commonly assessed.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Indications
content: Vascular ultrasound supports preinterventional and postinterventional assessment. Procedures frequently evaluated include transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), angioplasty, venoplasty, and stent placement. Lymph node ultrasound is indicated for palpable lymphadenopathy, concern for metastatic disease (eg, breast cancer), evaluation of infection (eg, tuberculosis), and procedural planning for fine needle aspiration cytology or biopsy in patients with systemic disease. [29]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Contraindications
content: Specific contraindications depend on the type of examination performed. Increased body habitus reduces sonographic evaluation accuracy due to greater impedance of the ultrasound wave. [30] Casts, dressings, or overlying surgical materials may further limit assessment. Extremity musculature, patient tremors, and voluntary or involuntary movement can compromise accurate Doppler evaluation of arterial and venous structures.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Equipment
content: Spatial resolution improves as sound wave frequency increases and wavelength decreases, although the ultrasound beam becomes more readily attenuated. Lower-frequency transducers (2.5–3.5 MHz) exhibit less attenuation and are, therefore, suitable for imaging deeper structures, such as renal or iliac arteries. The tradeoff is reduced spatial resolution with lower frequency transducers. Higher-frequency transducers (7–10 MHz) provide superior spatial resolution but have limited tissue penetration. These transducers are optimal for superficial vasculature or soft tissue structures, such as finger tendons. Transducer selection for lymph node evaluation depends on anatomic location.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Equipment
content: Ultrasound systems capable of both B-mode ("B" stands for "brightness") and Doppler imaging are recommended for quantifying stenosis. B-mode ultrasonography evaluates anatomy, including vessel caliber and morphology, whereas Doppler ultrasonography measures blood flow velocity, as described above.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Preparation
content: Preparation depends on the type of examination being performed. Regardless of the procedure, prior imaging should always be reviewed by both the clinician and technologist. Any casts, dressings, or overlying materials that could interfere with the examination should be removed whenever possible. [31] If removal is not feasible, the technologist must communicate this information to the interpreting clinician. The technologist should introduce themselves and verify the patient's name, date of birth, and institution-specific medical identifiers. All questions regarding diagnosis, treatment, or prognosis should be referred to the patient’s physician.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment
content: Ultrasound protocols and techniques vary according to the examination performed. Extremity arterial studies require anatomical assessment from proximal to distal. Both longitudinal and transverse images in B-mode and Doppler mode should be acquired. Optimization of gain, scale, and Doppler angle is essential for accurate velocity measurements. Waveform characteristics, including triphasic, biphasic, and monophasic patterns, should be documented along with corresponding velocities. Color Doppler imaging should be used to identify areas of aliasing or turbulence, indicative of hemodynamically significant stenosis. When stenosis is detected, 3 sets of velocities should be obtained immediately proximal to, within, and distal to the stenotic segment. [32]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Technique or Treatment
content: Extremity venous studies also require proximal-to-distal anatomical assessment. Calf veins are not routinely evaluated for DVT, as these vessels have a lower propensity to cause clinically significant thrombosis. [33] Veins should be interrogated with interval compression using the transducer to evaluate for thrombus. Color Doppler complements grayscale imaging by confirming the presence or absence of intraluminal flow in suspected thrombosed segments. Incompressibility should be documented (see Image . Popliteal Vein Compressibility). Flow augmentation should be performed for each interrogated vein, and the presence or absence of phasicity should be recorded.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: Vascular ultrasound is susceptible to artifacts that can complicate the evaluation of pathology. Artifacts arise from both instrument limitations and improper instrument settings. Recognition is essential to prevent misdiagnosis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: Aliasing produces a wrap-around defect on the Doppler display. When blood flow velocity exceeds the selected velocity range, the peak velocity is truncated and displayed on the opposite edge of the spectrum. On color Doppler, aliasing manifests as an abrupt color change, such as from blue to red, without a corresponding black stripe to indicate flow reversal. Increasing the velocity scale can eliminate aliasing or “wrap-around” artifacts. Areas of stenosis, which produce increased peak systolic velocities, are particularly prone to aliasing (see Image . Aliasing Artifact).

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: Low-velocity flow regions may not be detected if the velocity scale is set excessively high relative to blood flow speed. Technologists must verify velocity settings to avoid misdiagnosis of slow-flow areas as thrombosis.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: Increasing gain on the ultrasound machine enhances the echogenicity of structures on grayscale imaging. Excessive gain may produce a “blooming” artifact when color Doppler is activated. [34] In this phenomenon, the color extends beyond the interrogated anatomy, masking adjacent structures. Blooming can obscure partial thrombi and is corrected by decreasing color gain. Conversely, insufficient gain may prevent visualization of spectral or color Doppler signals. Optimal gain is achieved by increasing gain until noise appears and then gradually reducing it until noise is minimized.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Complications
content: Spectral broadening is a normal finding in areas of turbulent flow and at vascular branching points. However, this observation may also result from several artifacts. Excessively large Doppler sample volumes relative to vessel size can produce spectral broadening, as slower velocities near the vessel wall and faster central velocities are simultaneously recorded. Smaller vessels are particularly susceptible due to limitations in the minimum Doppler sample volume. Placement of the Doppler sample near the vessel wall also introduces slower velocity components, contributing to spectral broadening. Increased gain settings may further exacerbate this artifact. Spectral broadening may be minimized by optimizing gain, selecting an appropriately sized Doppler sample volume, and positioning the sample in the center of the vessel.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance
content: Extremity arterial stenosis is a commonly encountered pathology in arterial sonography. Ultrasound characteristics include the following: Increased PSV PSV ratio greater than 2, indicating more than 50% stenosis PSV ratio greater than 3, indicating more than 70% stenosis Waveform change from triphasic to monophasic from proximal to distal Spectral broadening distal to the stenosis Parvus tardus waveform distal to the stenosis Complete absence of flow, indicating total occlusion Color Doppler demonstrating flow turbulence or aliasing at the stenotic site DVT is a frequently encountered pathology in venous duplex imaging. Ultrasound characteristics include the following: Incompressibility of the thrombosed venous segment [35] Dilated venous lumen in acute DVT and contracted lumen in chronic DVT Loss of phasicity distal to thrombosis, including with the Valsalva maneuver Absence of color Doppler flow Loss of flow augmentation

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance
content: Lymphadenopathy is commonly observed and may result from malignant or reactive processes. Ultrasound features suggestive of malignancy include the following: Absence of a fatty hilum Cystic necrosis within the lymph node Long axis-to-short axis ratio less than 2, correlating with a rounder lymph node [36] Increased lymph node size, with thresholds varying by anatomical location Resistive index greater than 0.8 High-resistance waveform within the lymph node Presence of calcifications [37] [38]

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Clinical Significance
content: Sonographic evaluation provides critical insights into the presence, severity, and hemodynamic impact of vascular and lymphatic pathology. Accurate interpretation of these findings improves patient outcomes and guides interventional planning.

title: Sonography Vascular and Lymphatic Assessment, Protocols, and Interpretation -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The use of point-of-care ultrasonography has increased in recent years. Studies demonstrate that a systematic, team-based approach with early ultrasound scanning facilitates timely and accurate diagnosis. [39] Ultrasound is highly operator-dependent. Therefore, adherence to standardized protocols and consistent interpretation is essential to ensure accuracy and reproducibility. Structured interprofessional communication within a team-based approach supports timely decision-making and coordinated patient management, thereby enhancing diagnostic confidence and improving clinical outcomes.
